title: Instruction set architectures: RISC vs CISC
summary: The contract between software and hardware.

layers.basics: An ISA defines the instructions a processor understands. RISC uses simple fixed-size instructions; CISC has complex variable ones.
layers.deeper: ARM, RISC-V (RISC) and x86 (CISC outside, RISC-like inside) are the common ISAs.
layers.expert: Load/store architecture, register count, addressing modes, endianness; micro-ops decouple CISC from execution; ISA extensions (SIMD, NEON, AVX).

layers.basics: Assembly writes machine instructions as short mnemonics: ADD, LOAD, JUMP.
layers.deeper: Used for boot code, interrupt handlers and tight loops; compilers generate it from C.
layers.expert: Calling conventions, stack frames, link register vs push return; reading compiler output reveals optimisation.

layers.basics: A datapath of registers, ALU and buses is steered by a control unit decoding each instruction.
layers.deeper: Single-cycle, multi-cycle and pipelined designs trade clock rate and complexity.
layers.expert: Hardwired vs microcoded control; critical path through instruction memory, regfile, ALU, data memory.

layers.basics: Pipelining overlaps instruction stages (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back) so one finishes every cycle.
layers.deeper: Hazards: structural, data (forward results), control (branch prediction).
layers.expert: Speedup ≈ number of stages minus stalls; forwarding paths; branch predictors reach >95% accuracy; out-of-order and superscalar designs.

title: Cache memory
summary: Small and fast copies of memory.

layers.basics: A cache keeps recently used data near the CPU because programs reuse data (locality).
layers.deeper: Organisation: direct-mapped, set-associative; block size; replacement policy.
layers.expert: AMAT=hit time+miss rate×miss penalty; write-through vs write-back; coherence protocols (MESI) in multicores.

layers.basics: Fast memory is small and costly; big memory is slow. The hierarchy gives the illusion of fast and large.
layers.deeper: Typical: registers <1 ns, L1 ~1 ns, L2 3–5 ns, L3 10–20 ns, DRAM ~80 ns, flash ~50 µs.
layers.expert: Bandwidth, latency and the memory wall; prefetching; NUMA.

title: Virtual memory
summary: Each program thinks it owns memory.

layers.basics: The OS and hardware map each program’s addresses to physical memory, protecting programs from each other.
layers.deeper: Page tables, TLB cache translations; page faults load pages from storage.
layers.expert: Multi-level page tables, huge pages, MMU/IOMMU, address space layout randomisation.

layers.basics: A microcontroller bundles a CPU, memory and peripherals (timers, ADC, serial) in one chip for controlling devices.
layers.deeper: ARM Cortex-M dominates; AVR (Arduino) and PIC remain common in education and small designs.
layers.expert: Harvard vs von Neumann, NVIC interrupt controller, memory map, flash wait states, clock tree, debug via SWD/JTAG.

title: GPIO
summary: Pins that read and write bits.

layers.basics: General-purpose input/output pins can be configured as inputs or outputs and used to blink an LED or read a button.
layers.deeper: Modes: push-pull, open-drain, pull-up/down, analog, alternate function.
layers.expert: Slew rate, drive strength, Schmitt-trigger inputs, debouncing in hardware/software.

layers.basics: An interrupt pauses the program when something happens (a pin changes, a timer expires) and runs a handler.
layers.deeper: Priorities and nesting; keep handlers short; shared data needs protection.
layers.expert: Interrupt latency, vector table, tail-chaining on Cortex-M; priority inversion; volatile and atomic access.

title: Timers and PWM
summary: Counting clocks; fake analog by switching.

layers.basics: A timer counts clock pulses; pulse-width modulation varies how long a pin is high, controlling brightness or motor speed.
layers.deeper: Duty cycle D sets average voltage D·Vcc; filters or inertia smooth it.
layers.expert: Input capture, output compare, dead-time insertion for half-bridges; PWM resolution=log₂(f_clk/f_pwm) bits.

title: ADC and DAC peripherals
summary: Reading and writing analog on a microcontroller.

layers.basics: Built-in ADCs read sensor voltages; DACs or PWM output them.
layers.deeper: Sample time, reference voltage and source impedance affect accuracy; DMA streams samples.
layers.expert: Oversampling+decimation raise effective bits; anti-alias filters; ratiometric measurement cancels reference drift.

layers.basics: UART sends bytes one bit at a time on a wire with agreed speed (baud), framed by start and stop bits.
layers.deeper: Used for consoles, GPS modules and Bluetooth modules; RS-232/RS-485 levels extend range.
layers.expert: Baud error tolerance ≈ ±3%; oversampling receiver; flow control RTS/CTS.

layers.basics: SPI uses a clock, two data lines and a chip select to move bytes fast between a master and peripherals.
layers.deeper: Modes 0–3 define clock polarity and phase; used for flash, displays, ADCs.
layers.expert: Full-duplex shift-register exchange; speeds to 50+ MHz; daisy-chain topologies.

layers.basics: I²C connects many chips on two wires (clock and data), each with its own address.
layers.deeper: Open-drain lines with pull-up resistors; speeds 100 kHz–3.4 MHz; ACK bits confirm delivery.
layers.expert: Arbitration and clock stretching; bus capacitance limits to 400 pF; rise-time requirement sets pull-up value.

title: CAN bus
summary: Robust differential bus for vehicles and industry.

layers.basics: CAN is a two-wire differential bus where many nodes share messages; messages carry priority.
layers.deeper: Used in cars (engine, brakes, battery); non-destructive arbitration on message ID.
layers.expert: Dominant/recessive bits, bit stuffing, CRC-15, error confinement, CAN-FD to 5–8 Mbit/s.

layers.basics: USB carries data and power over one cable; the host polls devices which present descriptors.
layers.deeper: Speeds 480 Mb/s (USB 2) to 40 Gb/s (USB4); USB-C adds orientation-independent connector and Power Delivery.
layers.expert: Differential signalling; enumeration; PD negotiates 5–48 V up to 240 W (EPR); CC pins carry configuration.

layers.basics: An RTOS switches between tasks predictably so deadlines are met.
layers.deeper: Priority-based preemptive scheduling, semaphores, queues; FreeRTOS and Zephyr are common.
layers.expert: Rate-monotonic analysis (utilisation bound n(2^{1/n}−1)), priority inheritance, worst-case execution time.

layers.basics: Sleep modes, slower clocks and turning off unused parts reduce power by factors of thousands.
layers.deeper: Duty-cycled devices spend most time asleep at µA; energy per task matters.
layers.expert: Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling P∝CV²f; leakage in deep sleep; energy harvesting; battery life=capacity/average current.

layers.basics: A driver hides a peripheral’s registers behind a clean software interface.
layers.deeper: Layering: register access → driver → application; DMA and interrupts keep the CPU free.
layers.expert: HAL vs LL libraries; kernel-space drivers on Linux; memory barriers; device-tree description.

layers.basics: Sensors give voltages or digital values; conditioning circuits (amplify, filter, level-shift) prepare them for the microcontroller.
layers.deeper: Examples: thermistor in divider, Hall sensor, accelerometer over I²C.
layers.expert: Bridge circuits and instrumentation amps; calibration and drift; sensor fusion filters.

layers.basics: Motors need more current than a pin supplies: use a transistor or H-bridge and a flyback diode, with PWM for speed.
layers.deeper: DC, stepper and servo motors each need a different driver.
layers.expert: H-bridge dead-time to avoid shoot-through; current sensing; back-EMF; encoder feedback closes the loop.

layers.basics: LED, LCD and OLED displays connect over parallel, SPI or I²C buses; a frame buffer holds pixels.
layers.deeper: Multiplexing LED matrices cuts pins; OLED pixels emit light, LCDs modulate a backlight.
layers.expert: Refresh rate and bandwidth; MIPI DSI for phone displays; display controllers with DMA.
